html:
Another classic design question:

Your public API must allow each API key 100 requests per minute. Extra requests get 429 Too Many Requests. The API runs on 10 servers behind a load balancer. How do you design the rate limiter?

A rate limiter protects your servers from overload, stops one client from hogging capacity that others need, slows down brute-force attacks on login forms, and keeps costs under control when each request is expensive. It sits in front of everything, so it must be correct (no client gets far more than its limit), fast (it runs on every request) and reliable (it must not take the API down with it).

The Naive Version

The first idea is a counter in memory:

private final Map<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

boolean allow(String apiKey) {
    // Reset every minute by a scheduled task.
    return counts.merge(apiKey, 1, Integer::sum) <= 100;
}

It has two problems.

Each server counts alone. The load balancer spreads a client's requests over 10 servers, and each one allows 100. The client gets up to 1,000 requests a minute. The count must be shared.

The window resets all at once. With a counter per calendar minute, a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00: 200 requests in two seconds, and the limiter is happy. That's the weakness of the fixed window.

So we need two decisions: which algorithm counts, and where the count lives.

The Algorithms

Fixed window

Count requests per calendar window (12:00 to 12:01, 12:01 to 12:02…) and reject above the limit.

  • Pros: one counter per client, trivial to build.
  • Cons: up to twice the limit around a window boundary.

Sliding window log

Keep the timestamp of every request. To decide, drop the timestamps older than one minute and count the rest.

  • Pros: exact. "100 in any 60 seconds" means exactly that.
  • Cons: stores up to 100 timestamps per client. With a million clients, that's a lot of memory.

Sliding window counter

Keep the fixed-window counts of the current and previous minute, and weigh the previous one by how much of it is still inside the last 60 seconds:

estimate = previous × (1 − elapsed / 60s) + current

At 12:01:15, 25% of the current minute has passed, so 75% of the previous minute still counts. With 80 requests last minute and 30 this minute: 80 × 0.75 + 30 = 90. Allowed.

  • Pros: two counters per client, and no boundary burst.
  • Cons: an approximation, since it assumes the previous minute's requests were spread evenly. In practice it's very close.

Token bucket

Each client has a bucket holding up to capacity tokens, refilled at a steady rate. Each request takes a token; with no token left, it's rejected.

  • Pros: allows short bursts (up to the capacity) while holding the average rate. Two numbers per client: tokens left and last refill time. This is what AWS, Stripe and most API gateways use.
  • Cons: two settings to tune instead of one.

Leaky bucket

Requests go into a queue that's processed at a fixed rate; when the queue is full, new requests are dropped.

  • Pros: a perfectly smooth outflow, great in front of a fragile downstream system.
  • Cons: requests wait instead of being answered at once, which suits traffic shaping more than an API's yes-or-no check.

Which one?

Algorithm Memory per client Bursts at the boundary Allows planned bursts Exact
Fixed window 1 counter Yes, up to 2× No Per window only
Sliding window log 1 entry a request No No Yes
Sliding window counter 2 counters No No Close
Token bucket 2 numbers No Yes, up to capacity Yes, for its rule
Leaky bucket A queue No No, it smooths Yes, for its rule

For a public API, the token bucket is the usual answer: clients get the steady rate they pay for, plus a little slack for bursts, like loading a page that fires 10 requests at once. If the requirement really is "never more than 100 in any 60 seconds", use the sliding window counter.

Where the Count Lives: a Shared Store

Every server must see the same count, so the counters go in a shared, fast store. Redis is the usual choice: it's in memory, it answers in well under a millisecond, and it can expire keys by itself.

Don't read, then write

The tempting code reads the count, checks it, and writes it back:

// Don't: two servers can read 99 at the same time, and both allow.
int count = redis.get(key);
if (count < 100) {
    redis.set(key, count + 1);
    return true;
}
return false;

Two servers can read 99 at the same moment, both allow, and both write 100: one request too many. Under load, many more slip through. The check and the update must be one atomic step.

A fixed window with INCR

Redis's INCR adds one and returns the new value atomically, so it's both the check and the update:

INCR rate:key_abc:202611161201
EXPIRE rate:key_abc:202611161201 60 NX

The minute is in the key, so each window gets a fresh counter, and EXPIRE … NX (Redis 7) sets the expiry only when the key is new. If INCR returns more than 100, reject. Send both commands in one round trip with a pipeline or a MULTI transaction, so a crash between them can't leave a counter without an expiry.

A token bucket with a Lua script

A token bucket reads two values, computes, and writes two values: that's several commands, so it needs a Lua script, which Redis runs atomically, with no other command in between:

-- KEYS[1]: the bucket. ARGV: capacity, refill rate per second, now in ms.
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now      = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local bucket = redis.call("HMGET", KEYS[1], "tokens", "updated")
local tokens  = tonumber(bucket[1]) or capacity
local updated = tonumber(bucket[2]) or now

-- Refill for the time that passed, up to the capacity.
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - updated) / 1000 * rate)

local allowed = tokens >= 1
if allowed then tokens = tokens - 1 end

redis.call("HSET", KEYS[1], "tokens", tokens, "updated", now)
redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / rate * 1000))
return { allowed and 1 or 0, math.floor(tokens) }

The expiry is the time a bucket takes to fill up again: after that, a missing bucket and a full one are the same, so idle clients cost no memory.

Pass now from the application servers only if their clocks are in sync. Otherwise, read Redis's own clock with redis.call("TIME") inside the script, so every server agrees on what time it is.

The Filter in the Application

The limiter runs before any business code. In Spring, a filter does it:

@Component
public class RateLimitFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private final RateLimiter limiter;

    public RateLimitFilter(RateLimiter limiter) {
        this.limiter = limiter;
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
                                    HttpServletResponse response,
                                    FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String apiKey = request.getHeader("X-Api-Key");
        Decision decision = limiter.tryAcquire(apiKey);

        response.setHeader("RateLimit-Limit", "100");
        response.setHeader("RateLimit-Remaining",
                String.valueOf(decision.remaining()));

        if (!decision.allowed()) {
            response.setStatus(429);
            response.setHeader("Retry-After",
                    String.valueOf(decision.retryAfterSeconds()));
            return;
        }
        chain.doFilter(request, response);
    }
}

Tell clients where they stand: 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header saying how many seconds to wait, and RateLimit-* headers on every response so well-behaved clients can slow down before they hit the wall.

Design Decisions Interviewers Ask About

What do you limit by? An API key or a user id is the fairest. Limiting by IP address is the fallback for anonymous traffic, but many users can share one address behind a company proxy or a mobile carrier, and one attacker can use many addresses. Often you combine them: a per-key limit for normal use, and a per-IP limit on the login endpoint against brute force.

Where does it run? At the API gateway or load balancer, it stops abuse before it costs you anything, and every service gets it for free. In the application, it can use business knowledge, like a stricter limit for the free plan or for an expensive endpoint. Large systems do both: a coarse limit at the edge, finer ones inside.

Different limits for different things. Real APIs have several rules at once: per second and per day, per endpoint, per plan. Each rule is one more counter, checked in the same script.

What if Redis is down? You must choose:

  • Fail open: allow every request. The API stays up, unprotected for a while. Usually the right choice for a public API.
  • Fail closed: reject every request. Safer for something like a login endpoint under attack, but Redis's outage becomes your outage.

Whatever you choose, give the Redis call a short timeout, a few milliseconds, so a slow Redis can't make every request slow.

Latency on every request. One round trip to Redis per request is usually fine, around a millisecond in the same data center. At very high traffic, each server can also keep a small local limit, or take tokens from Redis in batches of 10, trading a little accuracy for far fewer calls.

Hot keys. One huge client can make one Redis key very busy. Redis Cluster spreads different keys across nodes, but a single key always lives on one node. For a giant client, split its limit across a few keys and pick one at random.

Every Failure, and What Happens

What goes wrong What happens Result
Requests spread over 10 servers All servers count in the same Redis key 100 a minute in total, not 1,000
Two servers check the same client at once INCR or the Lua script is atomic No request slips through
A burst at the end and start of a window The token bucket or sliding window counter has no reset moment No 2× burst
Server clocks drift apart The script reads Redis's own clock Every server agrees
A client goes quiet Its key expires No memory used for idle clients
Redis is slow or down A short timeout, then fail open (or closed for sensitive endpoints) The API stays up, or stays protected
A client hits the limit 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers It knows when to try again

The Answer in Short

  1. Pick the algorithm: a token bucket to allow short bursts around a steady rate, or a sliding window counter for a strict "N in any minute".
  2. Keep the counters in Redis, shared by every server, with an expiry so idle clients cost nothing.
  3. Make the check and the update atomic: INCR for a fixed window, a Lua script for a token bucket. Never read, then write.
  4. Run it first, in a filter or at the gateway, and answer 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers.
  5. Decide what happens when Redis fails, open or closed, and keep its timeout short.
